---
title: "VAR analysis"
subtitle: "Industrial production and University of Michigan consumer sentiment"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/setup.R")

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tseries)  # adf.test
  library(urca)     # ur.kpss, ca.jo
  library(vars)     # VARselect, VAR, causality, irf, fevd
})

umc_ts <- read_monthly_ts("data/umcsent.csv")

fmt_p <- function(p) {
  if (p < 2.2e-16) return("< 2.2e-16")
  if (p < 0.001) return(paste("=", format(p, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE)))
  paste("=", sprintf("%.4f", p))
}

# Johansen test statistics next to their critical values
johansen_table <- function(jo) {
  data.frame(
    Hypothesis = rownames(jo@cval),
    Statistic = round(jo@teststat, 2),
    jo@cval,
    check.names = FALSE,
    row.names = NULL
  )
}
```

The second series is the University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment
(UMCSENT), a monthly survey of how US households see current and future
economic conditions. The question is whether consumer sentiment carries
information about future industrial production.

## Consumer sentiment

```{r}
#| label: fig-umcsent
#| fig-cap: "University of Michigan consumer sentiment (1966:Q1 = 100)"
autoplot(umc_ts) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (1966:Q1 = 100)")
```

Unlike industrial production, sentiment has no clear upward trend but large
cyclical swings. It falls in the 2001 recession, the 2008–2009 financial crisis
and the 2020 pandemic; its lowest value in the sample is `r min(umc_ts)`
(`r format(zoo::as.yearmon(time(umc_ts)[which.min(umc_ts)]))`).

## Stationarity of UMCSENT

```{r}
#| label: tbl-umc-tests
#| tbl-cap: "KPSS statistics and ADF p-values, UMCSENT in levels"
umc_kpss <- sapply(c(tau = "tau", mu = "mu"), function(type) ur.kpss(umc_ts, type = type)@teststat)

adf_lags <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 24)
umc_adf <- data.frame(
  Lag = adf_lags,
  `ADF p-value` = sapply(adf_lags, function(k) suppressWarnings(adf.test(umc_ts, k = k)$p.value)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
umc_pp <- PP.test(umc_ts)

umc_adf
```

1. The KPSS statistics (`r round(umc_kpss["tau"], 4)` with trend and
   `r round(umc_kpss["mu"], 4)` with a constant) are above the 5% critical
   values (0.146 and 0.463), so stationarity in levels is rejected.
2. All ADF p-values are above 0.05 and the Phillips-Perron test gives
   p `r fmt_p(umc_pp$p.value)`, so the unit root cannot be rejected.

All three tests agree: UMCSENT is not stationary in levels.

## Cointegration (Johansen test)

```{r}
#| label: johansen
dset <- cbind(ip_ts, umc_ts)
colnames(dset) <- c("IPB", "UMCSENT")

lag_select <- VARselect(dset, lag.max = 8, type = "const")
lag_select$selection

johansen_trace <- ca.jo(dset, type = "trace", ecdet = "const", K = 4)
johansen_eigen <- ca.jo(dset, type = "eigen", ecdet = "const", K = 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-johansen
#| tbl-cap: "Johansen test: trace (top) and maximum eigenvalue (bottom)"
jo_trace <- johansen_table(johansen_trace)
jo_eigen <- johansen_table(johansen_eigen)
jo_trace
jo_eigen
```

For r = 0, both the trace statistic (`r jo_trace$Statistic[2]`) and the maximum
eigenvalue statistic (`r jo_eigen$Statistic[2]`) are below their 5% critical
values (`r jo_trace[["5pct"]][2]` and `r jo_eigen[["5pct"]][2]`). The null
hypothesis r = 0 cannot be rejected: there is no cointegrating relationship, so
no stable long-run link between industrial production and consumer sentiment.
A VECM is therefore not estimated; instead, a VAR is fitted to the first
differences of both series to make them stationary.

## First differences

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diff-tests
#| tbl-cap: "ADF and Phillips-Perron p-values for the differenced series"
dset_diff <- data.frame(
  IPB_d = diff(as.numeric(ip_ts)),
  UMCSENT_d = diff(as.numeric(umc_ts))
)

diff_tests <- data.frame(
  Series = names(dset_diff),
  `ADF p-value` = sapply(dset_diff, function(x) suppressWarnings(adf.test(x)$p.value)),
  `PP p-value` = sapply(dset_diff, function(x) PP.test(x)$p.value),
  check.names = FALSE,
  row.names = NULL
)
diff_tests
```

For both differenced series the ADF and Phillips-Perron p-values are 0.01
(below 0.05), so the unit root is rejected: both series are stationary after
differencing and can be used in the VAR.

## VAR lag selection and estimation

```{r}
#| label: var
var_lag <- VARselect(dset_diff, lag.max = 12, type = "const")
var_lag$selection

var_model <- VAR(dset_diff, p = 4, type = "const")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-var-ipb
#| tbl-cap: "VAR(4), equation for the change in industrial production (IPB_d)"
var_summary <- summary(var_model)
ipb_eq <- var_summary$varresult$IPB_d$coefficients
umc_eq <- var_summary$varresult$UMCSENT_d$coefficients
round(ipb_eq, 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-var-umc
#| tbl-cap: "VAR(4), equation for the change in consumer sentiment (UMCSENT_d): lags of IPB_d"
round(umc_eq[grep("^IPB_d", rownames(umc_eq)), ], 4)
```

1. The information criteria suggest 12 lags; p = 4 is used to keep the model
   parsimonious and easy to interpret.
2. In the industrial production equation, sentiment one month earlier
   (`UMCSENT_d.l1`) has a positive coefficient
   (`r round(ipb_eq["UMCSENT_d.l1", "Estimate"], 3)`) that is significant at 5%
   (p `r fmt_p(ipb_eq["UMCSENT_d.l1", "Pr(>|t|)"])`): an improvement in consumer
   confidence is followed by higher industrial production the next month.
3. In the sentiment equation, none of the lags of industrial production is
   significant.

The VAR(4) suggests a one-directional short-run relationship, from consumer
sentiment to industrial production.

## VAR diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: var-diagnostics
var_serial <- serial.test(var_model, lags.pt = 20, type = "PT.asymptotic")
var_arch <- vars::arch.test(var_model, lags.multi = 12, multivariate.only = TRUE)
var_norm <- normality.test(var_model, multivariate.only = TRUE)

data.frame(
  Test = c("Portmanteau (autocorrelation, 20 lags)", "Multivariate ARCH (12 lags)", "Jarque-Bera (normality)"),
  `p-value` = signif(c(
    var_serial$serial$p.value,
    var_arch$arch.mul$p.value,
    var_norm$jb.mul$JB$p.value
  ), 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cusum
#| fig-cap: "OLS-CUSUM stability test for each VAR equation"
#| fig-height: 6
stability_model <- stability(var_model, type = "OLS-CUSUM")
plot(stability_model)
```

The diagnostic tests all give p < 0.05, indicating residual autocorrelation,
ARCH effects and non-normality, which reflect the macroeconomic shocks of
1990–2025. In the OLS-CUSUM plot, the empirical fluctuation process stays
within the critical bands for both equations, so the parameters of the VAR(4)
are stable over the sample. The model is used for the causality analysis and the
forecast below.

## Granger causality

```{r}
#| label: tbl-granger
#| tbl-cap: "Granger causality tests (F-tests on all four lags)"
granger_ipb <- causality(var_model, cause = "IPB_d")
granger_umc <- causality(var_model, cause = "UMCSENT_d")

data.frame(
  Direction = c("IPB_d -> UMCSENT_d", "UMCSENT_d -> IPB_d"),
  `F statistic` = round(c(granger_ipb$Granger$statistic, granger_umc$Granger$statistic), 4),
  `p-value` = round(c(granger_ipb$Granger$p.value, granger_umc$Granger$p.value), 4),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

1. IPB_d → UMCSENT_d: p `r fmt_p(granger_ipb$Granger$p.value)` (> 0.05); changes
   in industrial production do not help predict consumer sentiment.
2. UMCSENT_d → IPB_d: the joint p-value for the four lags is
   `r round(granger_umc$Granger$p.value, 4)` (> 0.05), so at the 5% level the
   null hypothesis of no Granger causality cannot be rejected.
3. The first lag of sentiment was individually significant in the VAR, but the
   Granger test evaluates all four lags together, and lags 2–4 are not
   significant, which weakens the joint F-test.

The information link between the two variables appears only at a very short
horizon (one month) and fades over a four-month window.

## Impulse response functions

```{r}
#| label: fig-irf-umc
#| fig-cap: "Response of IPB_d to a shock in UMCSENT_d (90% bootstrap bands)"
set.seed(123)  # bootstrap confidence bands
irf_umc_to_ipb <- irf(
  var_model,
  impulse = "UMCSENT_d",
  response = "IPB_d",
  n.ahead = 20,
  boot = TRUE,
  ci = 0.90
)
plot(irf_umc_to_ipb, main = "Shock to UMCSENT_d, response of IPB_d")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-irf-ipb
#| fig-cap: "Response of UMCSENT_d to a shock in IPB_d (90% bootstrap bands)"
irf_ipb_to_umc <- irf(
  var_model,
  impulse = "IPB_d",
  response = "UMCSENT_d",
  n.ahead = 20,
  boot = TRUE,
  ci = 0.90
)
plot(irf_ipb_to_umc, main = "Shock to IPB_d, response of UMCSENT_d")
```

1. A positive shock to consumer sentiment raises industrial production in the
   following month, and the effect is statistically significant (the bootstrap
   band is entirely above zero). The effect is temporary and dies out after
   about five months.
2. For a shock to industrial production, the zero line stays inside the
   confidence band: production shocks have no significant effect on consumer
   confidence.

This supports the view of sentiment indicators as leading indicators of real
industrial activity.

## Forecast error variance decomposition

```{r}
#| label: fig-fevd
#| fig-cap: "Forecast error variance decomposition (10 months)"
#| fig-height: 6
fevd_result <- fevd(var_model, n.ahead = 10)
plot(fevd_result)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fevd
#| tbl-cap: "Share of forecast error variance at a 10-month horizon"
fevd_10 <- rbind(
  IPB_d = fevd_result$IPB_d[10, ],
  UMCSENT_d = fevd_result$UMCSENT_d[10, ]
)
round(100 * fevd_10, 2)
```

1. In the first month, almost 100% of the variance of each variable is
   explained by its own shocks.
2. At a 10-month horizon, changes in consumer sentiment explain about
   `r round(100 * fevd_10["IPB_d", "UMCSENT_d"], 2)`% of the forecast error
   variance of industrial production.
3. In the other direction, industrial production explains only
   `r round(100 * fevd_10["UMCSENT_d", "IPB_d"], 2)`% of the variance of
   consumer sentiment.

The decomposition supports a one-sided, short-run relationship: sentiment plays
a small but stable role as a leading indicator for industry.

## VAR forecast

```{r}
#| label: fig-var-forecast
#| fig-cap: "VAR forecast of industrial production, 24 months ahead (dashed line = end of data)"
var_forecast <- predict(var_model, n.ahead = 24, ci = 0.90)

fc_ipb_diff <- var_forecast$fcst$IPB_d[, "fcst"]

# Rebuild index levels by adding the forecast changes to the last observed value
last_ipb <- tail(as.numeric(ip_ts), 1)
fc_ipb_level <- cumsum(c(last_ipb, fc_ipb_diff))[-1]

history_time <- as.numeric(time(ip_ts))
last_time_point <- tail(history_time, 1)
forecast_time <- seq(last_time_point + 1 / 12, by = 1 / 12, length.out = length(fc_ipb_level))

df_ipb <- data.frame(
  time = c(history_time, forecast_time),
  value = c(as.numeric(ip_ts), fc_ipb_level)
)

ggplot(df_ipb, aes(x = time, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = last_time_point, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)")
```

1. `predict()` forecasts the next 24 months with a 90% interval.
2. Because the VAR is estimated on differences, the forecasts are monthly
   changes.
3. They are converted back to index levels with `cumsum()`, adding the forecast
   changes to the last observed value (`r round(last_ipb, 2)`).
4. To the right of the dashed red line, industrial production grows steadily and
   moderately, to `r round(tail(fc_ipb_level, 1), 2)` after 24 months, supported
   by the positive impulse from consumer sentiment.
